hints: Focus on what favours sharing electrons rather than losing them, small non-metal atoms with high electronegativity.
Sort the four elements into metals, metalloid or non-metal, and noble gas to see who wants to share.
Think about which element forms classic molecular chlorides and fluorides like $\text{BCl}_3$ and decide which list fits best.
walkthrough:
**Recall what favours covalent bonding**

Covalent bonding means sharing electrons. It is favoured by non-metals and metalloids that are small and quite electronegative, so they hold onto electrons instead of giving them away.

**Classify each element**

Boron, $\text{B}$, is a Group 13 metalloid with non-metal character. Magnesium, $\text{Mg}$, and potassium, $\text{K}$, are s-block metals that easily lose electrons to form $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{K}^{+}$. Neon, $\text{Ne}$, is a Group 18 noble gas with a full octet.

**Compare their typical chemistry**

$\text{K}$ and $\text{Mg}$ form ionic compounds such as $\text{KCl}$ and $\text{MgO}$. $\text{Ne}$ forms essentially no compounds. Boron forms classic covalent molecules by sharing its three outer electrons:
$$\text{B} + 3\text{Cl} \rightarrow \text{BCl}_3$$
So boron has by far the greatest covalent tendency.

options.A: Boron is small, quite electronegative and a metalloid. It does not easily form B3+ ions, so it shares electrons to complete its octet, forming covalent molecules such as BF3, BCl3 and B2H6.
options.B: Magnesium is a Group 2 metal with low electronegativity. It readily loses two electrons to form Mg2+, giving predominantly ionic compounds like MgCl2 and MgO, so its covalent tendency is much lower than boron.
options.C: Neon has a complete octet (1s2 2s2 2p6) and very high ionisation energy. It has no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons under normal conditions, so it forms essentially no compounds, covalent or ionic.
options.D: Potassium is a Group 1 alkali metal with very low electronegativity and low ionisation energy. It very easily loses one electron to form K+, giving strongly ionic compounds like KCl and K2O, the opposite of covalent behaviour.
